rv.q: It’s an affecting tale but not entirely bleak.
Yet Amit Sharma’s production, threaded through with folk song, has, for all its terrors, an element of fable – and of a modest, truthful piece of theatre blinking in the semi-commercial glare.
But in its determination to tell a neatly rounded story, it neglects other, less palatable, less familiar truths.
Yet often, sad to say, it’s the very goodness of the Amiris in this telling that works against a true sense of the horror of what they go through.
There’s a sheer moral clarity to its directness, even if it is inescapably flawed theatre.
Hardship has seldom seemed so easily borne as at the National Theatre this week, where a brace of plays make light work of the rigours of discrimination, poverty and displacement.
The Amiri family's story is remarkable — though sadly, all too common — and this production serves as a fitting reminder of both the plight and humanity of all who undertake such a perilous journey.
The play is heartfelt and heartwarming, twice over.

Yet this theatrical retelling feels frustratingly underpowered and sadly overshadowed by the new stories emerging daily from a country that once more has proved that, for better or worse, it will always be a law unto itself.

I confess to tiring somewhat of the cutesier passages where things are told rather than shown and where we are informed rather unnecessarily that the tale on view “is about all of us”, lest playgoers think they can distance themselves from the determination on view.
Phil Porter’s adaptation of Hamed and Hessam’s book is sadly littered with clunky dialogue – so full of exposition that it blights the drama and the emotional core of the play.
Charming, but ultimately middle-of-the-road verging on saccharine, The Boy With Two Hearts’ lack of depth is a real pity...

cn.t: Critics find this true story of an Afghan family's refugee journey moving and timely, but fault the production for being overly simple and saccharine, with staging that doesn't match the emotional weight of its subject matter.
